statements.quote: A feedforward network answers one question and forgets it.
The token that left the model's mind is gone — the next token is produced without the first one having made a mark.
But language is *sequential*: the meaning of “was” arrives only with what came before.
\citeauthor{colah2015lstm}'s classic walkthrough (\citeyear{colah2015lstm}) puts it simply:
> Humans don't start their thinking from scratch every second.
… You don't throw everything away and start thinking from scratch again.
Your thoughts have persistence.
A **recurrent neural network (RNN)** gives a network the same trick: a loop that feeds its own hidden state back in.
Instead of a stack of layers, it is a chain of copies of one network, each passing a **hidden state** $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ to the next — the machine keeps reading its own writing.
The loop is older than the language model.

\citeauthor{hopfield1982} showed that a network of symmetrically connected threshold units could store patterns as stable states of an energy landscape, with the dynamics settling into one of them \cite{hopfield1982}.

Hopfield's networks were not trained by backpropagation and did not process sequences token by token, but they established the idea the RNN inherits: a network's computation can be a trajectory through state space rather than a single feedforward pass.
The recurrence is easiest to read when it is **unrolled** across time — drawn as a sequence of identical networks, one per step, each handing its state forward:
The recurrent loop unfolded as a chain — $\mathbf{a}$ is the input, $\mathbf{h}$ the state the copies hand to each other, $\mathbf{y}$ the output.
[Diagram: fdeloche, CC BY-SA 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Recurrent_neural_network_unfold.svg)
“Recurrent” hides a beautiful fact: the *same* weight matrices $\mathbf{W}_h$, $\mathbf{W}_x$ are used at **every** step.
There is one network, applied many times.

This is the weight-sharing trick from the [computer vision chapter](computer_vision.php) — a filter that slides over time instead of over space (see also the fixed-weight argument in \cite[Olah, 2014]{colah2014conv}).
It is also why \citeauthor{colah2015lstm} calls RNNs “intimately related to sequences and lists”: they are *the* natural architecture for data that arrives one step at a time.
The first trainable recurrent architectures came from psychology and connectionism.

\citeauthor{jordan1986} added *context units* that copied the previous output back into the input, and \citeauthor{elman1990finding} made the hidden layer itself recurrent, giving the network a memory of its own internal state \cite{jordan1986,elman1990finding}.
Elman called his model a *simple recurrent network*; it is essentially the recurrence above, trained by backpropagation through the unrolled chain.
These small networks learned grammar-like regularities in sequences—and set the stage for the vanishing-gradient diagnosis that followed.
Because the state must be *propagated* — multiplied through the chain, step by step — far-apart context is fragile.
Predicting the next word in *“the clouds are in the sky”* needs only recent words.
But finish *“I grew up in France … I speak fluent __”*, and the answer depends on something from sentences ago.
In the long gap, an RNN must remember the word “France” while doing all the intervening work.
\citeauthor{colah2015lstm} captures the state of things precisely:
> In theory, RNNs are absolutely capable of handling such “long-term dependencies.” … In practice, RNNs don't seem to be able to learn them.
The failure mode is the [vanishing gradient](backproplab.php).

Unrolling an RNN computes gradients through many multiplications of the same matrix; if the Jacobian's spectral radius stays below 1, the signal *shrinks* toward zero — mathematically, a long step sequence compounds the decay into the exponential $\rho^{k}$ that [attention later sidesteps entirely](attentionlab.php) \cite{colah2015backprop,hochreiter1991vanishing}.

The problem was diagnosed early by \citeauthor{hochreiter1991vanishing} (\citeyear{hochreiter1991vanishing}) and formalized for recurrent networks by \citeauthor{bengio1994learning} (\citeyear{bengio1994learning}) — but the fix arrived as an explicit memory.
Training a recurrent net means differentiating through the unrolled graph, a procedure known as **backpropagation through time**.
\citeauthor{werbos1990bptt} gave the method its canonical exposition, showing how the adjoint recurrence runs backward along the same chain that generated the states \cite{werbos1990bptt}.

In the language of the [autodiff chapter](autodiff.php), BPTT is simply reverse-mode AD applied to a graph whose depth is the sequence length—which is exactly why the same vanishing-gradient arithmetic returns.
The **Long Short-Term Memory** network, introduced by \citeauthorlastnameand{lstm} in \citeyear{lstm}, changes what flows down the chain \cite{lstm}.
Alongside the ordinary hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$ runs a **cell state** $\mathbf{c}_t$ — a lane that is *not* transformed by every gate.
\citeauthor{colah2015lstm} calls it the conveyor belt: information rides on it straight through the network, altered only by the gentle, learned interactions that **gates** apply.
Each gate is a sigmoid layer whose output lies in $[0,1]$ — it reads “how much to let through,” from closed ($0$) to wide open ($1$) \cite{colah2015lstm}.
The original LSTM had an input gate and an output gate; the forget gate was added by \citeauthor{lstm_vanilla} (\citeyear{lstm_vanilla}).
The modern cell has three:
The cell update is then a soft overwrite, not a full rewrite:
In a language model that has learned grammar, \citeauthor{colah2015lstm} notes the gates learn an interpretable job:
> …it might output whether the subject is singular or plural, so that we know what form a verb should be conjugated into if that's what follows next.

Forget the gate, keep the memory: that is the whole trick — an *elementwise* multiplication by a gate near 1 instead of a full matrix product, so the gradients survive the journey across a long sentence \cite{colah2015lstm}.
The LSTM was not invented in a vacuum.

In his 1991 diploma thesis, \citeauthor{hochreiter1991vanishing} analyzed why recurrent gradients decay; the solution he and Schmidhuber developed, the *constant error carousel*, appeared in the 1997 LSTM paper \cite{hochreiter1991vanishing,lstm}.
The carousel is a self-connected unit whose error signal can flow backward without being multiplied by a weight matrix—the cell state made trainable.
Learned input and output gates let the network decide when to write to it and when to read from it.

The LSTM's dominance in speech came from **Alex Graves** and colleagues' **CTC** loss (2006), which let a recurrent network learn to align an unsegmented acoustic signal with its transcript; CTC-LSTM became the first end-to-end neural speech recogniser to beat the classical pipeline, and by 2015 it was running Google's Android speech recognition \cite{ctc2006}.
A single LSTM cell: the cell state runs along the top, while the forget, input and output gates decide what is kept, written and read.
Diagram: fdeloche, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Long_Short-Term_Memory.svg).
What follows is a pruning of the idea, not a new invention.

The **gated recurrent unit (GRU)** of \citeauthor{cho2014gru} (\citeyear{cho2014gru}) merges the forget and input gates into one **update gate**, and weds the memory to the output via a **reset gate** — two gates instead of three, fewer parameters, similar performance \cite{cho2014gru}.

And when \citeauthor{greff2015lstm} and colleagues *searched* the space of LSTM variants systematically, they reached a deflating but reassuring conclusion: the best variants are only marginally better than the plain, standard LSTM \cite{greff2015lstm}.

The message of that search echoes [the universality discussion in the toolkit](https://asanai.scads.ai): architecture cleverness buys freedom from *unavoidable* failure, but the winning configurations cluster together — “all about the same” \cite{colah2015lstm}.
What actually scaled, as [the next chapter](attentionlab.php) shows, was not a better gate but *removing the chain entirely* — \citeauthor{colah2015lstm} ends his walkthrough with an honest roadmap:
> A common opinion among researchers is: "Yes!
There is a next step and it's attention!" The idea is to let every step of an RNN pick information to look at from some larger collection of information.
The recurrent loop becomes much more useful when you give it a job with two different sequences.

**Sequence-to-sequence** learning (seq2seq), introduced in 2014 by Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le and independently by Cho et al., pairs two recurrent networks (\cite[Sutskever et al., 2014]{sutskever2014seq2seq}; \cite[Cho et al., 2014]{cho2014gru}):
The context vector is the paradigm's central wager: that the meaning of a sentence of any length can be stored as a point in a fixed-dimensional space, and unfolded back into another language.
It is also its central weakness.
Everything the decoder knows about the source must pass through those few numbers, so quality falls as sentences get longer.
Sutskever et al. found a cheap partial fix: **reverse the source sentence**, which puts the first source words — the ones that predict the first target words — close to the context vector.

That per-step alignment is the direct ancestor of the self-attention inside every Transformer: instead of one compressed summary, the decoder learns *where to look* (\cite[Bahdanau et al., 2014]{bahdanau2014}).
Training introduced a protocol that every modern language model still uses.

**Teacher forcing** feeds the decoder the *true* previous token at every step, not its own prediction, so all positions can be scored in one parallel pass; the technique goes back to \citeauthor{williams1989} (\citeyear{williams1989}).
At inference the gold prefix is gone and the model consumes its own outputs; the mismatch between the two conditions is called **exposure bias**.
Scheduled sampling, which gradually replaces gold tokens with model predictions during training, was the recurrent era's remedy \cite{bengio2015scheduled}.
At Transformer scale the problem largely receded in practice, but the protocol did not: next-token training *is* teacher forcing with a causal mask.
The seq2seq form outlived the recurrence.

Google's production GNMT system stacked eight LSTM layers per side \cite{wu2016gnmt}, the Transformer kept the encoder–decoder skeleton and replaced the recurrent core with attention \cite{vaswani2017attention}, T5 recast every task as text-to-text \cite{raffel2020t5}, and Whisper carried the same shape into speech recognition \cite{radford2022whisper}.
